Short-term Treasury bills (T-Bills) could also be considered for their liquidity and low risk.

For laddered maturity structure, I suggest allocating 30% of the portfolio to bonds maturing in year 1, 25% in year 2, 20% in year 3, and 10% each in years 4 and 5, with the remaining 5% in bonds with a 10-year maturity. This distribution ensures that no single year accounts for more than 30% of maturity, adhering to the constraint. Within the government bond allocation, I propose investing 20% in short-term (1-2 year) Treasuries to lock in predictable returns and 10% in ultra-long (10-15 year) Treasuries to provide a long-term cushion. The corporate bond allocation will be split between 20% in high-grade corporate bonds (BBB+/Aaa rated) with a 5-year coupon, securing relatively stable yields and 10% in investment-grade corporate bonds with a 7-year coupon to achieve a balanced risk profile. The proposed laddered maturity structure allows for regular reinvestment of principal and interest, facilitating gradual, incremental returns without overexposure to interest rate fluctuations.
